title: cmHC: Balancing Stream Mixing in Hyper-Connections via Geometric Contraction

details.title: cmHC: Balancing Stream Mixing in Hyper-Connections via Geometric Contraction
details.abstract: Manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) extends residual connections to multiple streams and stabilizes residual propagation by constraining stream-mixing residual matrices to the Birkhoff polytope, the set of doubly stochastic matrices. In this work, we investigate how to effectively mix residual streams within the Birkhoff polytope . We reveal a mixing trade-off : when under-mixed residual matrices stay close to the vertices of the Birkhoff polytope, hyper-connections will degenerate into a set of nearly independent streams; when over-mixe d residual matrices are concentrated around the uniform barycenter of the polytope, streams will become less distinguishable from each other. We theoretically validate our findings by bounding the cumulative residual mixing, stream difference and gradient difference of mixing coefficients across layers. Motivated by these findings, we propose Contraction for Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (cmHC), an exact doubly stochastic method which geometrically contracts the Birkhoff polytope toward its interior. This contraction mitigates under-mixing by forcing the residual matrices to explore deeper into the polytope, with a provable stream mixing bound and no new parameterization. Moreover, we apply a moderate contraction at the shallow layers to prevent over-mixing, enabling stable gradient propagation on extremely large-scale model pretraining. Extensive experiments across dense and mixture-of-experts models at various parameter scales demonstrate the effectiveness and scalability of cmHC. We also develop fused operators for cmHC on Ascend NPUs, reducing hyper-connection execution latency by up to 44.8%.

title: Non-penetrating World Models

details.title: Non-penetrating World Models
details.abstract: 🚧 World models can generate amazing worlds, but they still walk through walls! 👻 🎮 Today's video world models can generate impressive interactive environments, but they often fail to respect basic physical boundaries. For example, when you press W toward a wall, the model may simply walk straight through it! 💡 We introduce NoPeWorld , a lightweight framework that helps video world models stop at obstacles instead of walking through them . Interestingly, we find that world models already encode collision information in their hidden states. NoPeWorld leverages this information to prevent physical violations without retraining the entire world model. 📊 We also introduce NoPeBench , a benchmark for evaluating whether world models respect physical boundaries. 🚀 Check out our demos and open-source resources! 🌐 Project & Demos | 💻 Code | 🤗 Dataset | 📄 Paper

title: Reading the Unreadable: Text-Aware Image Super-Resolution Needs Reasoning

details.title: Reading the Unreadable: Text-Aware Image Super-Resolution Needs Reasoning
details.abstract: [TL;DR] Text-aware image super-resolution (TAISR) needs reasoning! Humans can often read badly degraded text by reasoning over context: a word repeated elsewhere in the image, neighboring numbers on a ruler, or a familiar logo. Super-resolution (SR) models rely on local visual evidence alone, so they struggle with exactly this kind of text. 🔍 ReasonText is a human-curated benchmark that separates reasoning-required text from locally recoverable text, paired with GTTCA , a recognition-based metric that measures text restoration without text-detection errors. Across 12 recent SR models, including TAISR models built for text, accuracy on reasoning-required text stays below 25%. 💡 RTC (Reasoning Transfer via Captioning) is a training-free plug-in. An MLLM reasons out the degraded text and writes it into the caption of a frozen text-conditioned SR model. RTC improves all six text-conditioned SR models we tested, especially on reasoning-required text (e.g., DiT4SR: 24.5% → 45.8%). Surprisingly, DiT4SR + RTC, a general real-world SR model, outperforms UniT + RTC, a TAISR model built on the same backbone with extra text-aware modules. This suggests that reasoning should be a core design axis for future TAISR. 🤗 Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Jasonleex1995/ReasonText 🌐 Project page: https://jasonleex1995.github.io/TAISR_needs_Reasoning/ 💻 Code: https://github.com/jasonleex1995/TAISR_needs_Reasoning 📍 Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. title: AgentRoboCritic: Understanding the Capability of Frontier Agents on Direct Robot Control

details.title: AgentRoboCritic: Understanding the Capability of Frontier Agents on Direct Robot Control
details.abstract: 🤖 Can frontier agents control robots directly with low-level actions? And how do we actually tell how good they are? 📉 Existing evaluations focus on episode-level scores such as success rates. They hide the action-level feedback that is key to improving embodied agents! 💡 We introduce AgentRoboCritic . The policy agent states a local intent alongside each action, and a critic evaluates every action against it. For a failed action, the critic also returns its failure mode. With GPT-6 Astra as the critic, we annotate 12,844 actions across 12 manipulation benchmarks. 🔍 What the action-level feedback reveals: Closed-loop recovery: 49.8% of successful episodes contain at least one failed action, and 57.7% of failed actions are recovered by the end of the episode. Reliable semantic grounding: acting on the wrong object, order or category accounts for only 0.2% of failed actions. Strong zero-shot manipulation: GPT-6 Astra succeeds in 91% of RoboTwin 2.0 and 90% of YAMLab episodes, where π0.5 reaches 6% and 0%. The remaining bottleneck is physical execution: Grasp is the leading failure mode on most benchmarks. 🚀 To make action-level feedback low-cost, we release the 12,844 annotated actions, a 400-action human-annotated benchmark, and a fine-tuned Muse-Glimmer-30B critic. Its failure-mode accuracy rises from 32.6% to 74.2%, at over 30× lower cost than GPT-6 Astra. 🌐 Project page | 💻 Code | 🤗 Dataset | 📊 Benchmark | 🧠 Critic model | 📄 Paper

Three rounds take a 2B VLA policy on TravelUAV from 46.4% to 67.5% success and halve its collisions, 10.6 points above AeroDPO (the prior SOTA baseline), with no extra human labels or inference cost. 🌐 Project page (with demo video): https://starsholic.github.io/AeroRSI/ 💻 Code: https://github.com/starsholic/AeroRSI 🤗 Models: https://huggingface.co/DavidWu1116/AeroRSI Happy to answer any questions!

details.title: Moving Generality from Model to Modeler: LLM Agents for PHM on a Deployment-Style Benchmark
details.abstract: Should generality live in the model, or in the agent that builds a model for each new machine? NextUnit-Bench tests coding agents on 24 PHM datasets with sealed evaluation on unseen machines. The best agents beat AutoML and foundation models, and often even state-of-the-art methods from the literature; their edge is a design made on the data, and the designs are strikingly plain: textbook methods, rarely deep networks. If agents can out-know and out-code most human experts, the next general model in PHM may not be a model at all.

title: Intent Contracts: Taking Tools Away from Agents

details.abstract: Instead of letting the agent write commands and having a classifier approve them, we take the tools away from the planner: it states its intent with a verbatim quote of the user, and a small trusted model writes every tool call. This gives a complete pre-action record and lets the trusted side do only the authorized part of a bundled request (27/30 vs 16/30 tasks completed). It did not reduce unauthorized actions compared with a blind command reviewer, and we report that as a main result. One model pair, benign over-reach only. title: PURE: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Multi-Granularity Multimodal Identity Matching

details.title: PURE: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Multi-Granularity Multimodal Identity Matching
details.abstract: Hi HF community! 👋 I’m one of the authors of PURE. Same design, different color: should two product listings count as a match? The answer depends on whether we care about the underlying product design or the specific variant. We introduce PURE , a diagnostic benchmark built from real-world e-commerce matching pairs , with 1,457 multiple-choice questions verified by domain experts across 14 tasks. It examines four capabilities involved in multimodal identity matching: Perception, Understanding, Reasoning, and Evidence-grounded Judgment , with explicit distinctions between base-level and variant-level matching. A few interesting findings from our evaluation of 10 multimodal LLMs: Understanding scores highest on average, while evidence-grounded judgment scores lowest. Locating visual differences and applying variant-level matching rules remain challenging. Models can incorrectly report attribute conflicts between records that actually match. The pattern changes with granularity: most models recognize matching pairs more accurately than non-matching pairs at the base level, while the reverse holds at the variant level. We hope PURE helps the community identify weaknesses that aggregate matching accuracy can hide, and provides a useful testbed for improving multimodal grounding and matching. 📊 Dataset and evaluation code We’d love to hear your thoughts and see how your models perform!

title: Taking Apart and Putting Together: Tracking Objects Through Physical Transformations

details.title: Taking Apart and Putting Together: Tracking Objects Through Physical Transformations
details.abstract: Video trackers like SAM 2/3 keep one identity per object, so they break when objects are taken apart or put together. We introduce Transformation Tracking and Understanding (TTU): tracking objects through physical assemblies and disassemblies while keeping a state graph of the transformation process. TIPO , a training-free framework that generates split/merge proposals, scores them against mask-decoder priors, and asks an MLLM to verify and label them. It's state-of-the-art on tracking and state-graph accuracy while running 6–15× faster than prior methods. VISTA , a new benchmark: 50 videos (IKEA ASM, Assembly101 and custom recordings) with dense masks and 256 annotated transformations (124 assemblies, 132 disassemblies). 🌐 Project page: https://davidegardenal.github.io/tipo-tracking 🤗 Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/davidegarde/VISTA

title: Exploited Before It Was Fixed? Vulnerability Timelines from Open, Machine-Readable Evidence

details.title: Exploited Before It Was Fixed? Vulnerability Timelines from Open, Machine-Readable Evidence
details.abstract: How long are vulnerabilities exploited before a fix is available? We compute, for each vulnerability, the interval between exploitation and patch, and lifecycle intervals adapted from the Vulnerability Timeline and Exposure Metrics framework (VTEM), from open, machine-readable evidence: CVE and CSAF records, publisher timelines (GCVE BCP-05-X-03), several Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogs and sightings. An evidence model selects the earliest evidence of each lifecycle event, uses only records that describe the vulnerability itself, carries the precision of every date and traces each figure to the record that produced it; it is implemented in Vulnerability-Lookup. Over the 3,758 identifiers with exploitation evidence on one instance, disclosure is dated for 98%, patch evidence exists for 15.7%, and the vendor-side dates VTEM requires are never published. Most exploitation dates are catalog listings, 1,041 of them on days a catalog listed or imported a backlog. Setting those and unordered same-day pairs aside, 59 vulnerabilities have patch evidence after exploitation evidence, by a median of 7.6 days, mostly from a catalog listing to a distributor’s fix. Traceability made the data correctable: one collector recorded exploit publications as exploitation, 40% of the exploitation dates of a first measurement, and one catalog dated 11% of its listings with the vulnerability’s publication time.

title: Search From the Start: Search-Native Pretraining for Language Models

details.title: Search From the Start: Search-Native Pretraining for Language Models
details.abstract: We introduce Search-Native Pretraining , a practical approach to teaching language models to search the web during pretraining. We augment ordinary text corpora with synthetic web-search queries, execute these queries against a local search index, and train language models to issue search calls and incorporate retrieved evidence into language modeling. Search-pretrained models ("QueryLM") are better at knowledge-intensive tasks and show higher steerability toward the retrieved evidence. Throughout our experiments, we find that a 1.4B QueryLM consistently beats or matches the performance of a FLOP-matched 3.3B baseline model across all knowledge intensive tasks. We release the training data and model checkpoints. Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26809v1 Models and data: https://huggingface.co/collections/Kausp11/search-native-pretraining

title: GameWM: Toward Next-Generation Video Games with Interaction-Centric World Models

details.title: GameWM: Toward Next-Generation Video Games with Interaction-Centric World Models
details.abstract: Hey everyone, Excited to share our new work, GameWM. We ask one question: if we design the next generation of games around the generative power of video models, what should a game's structure look like? From that answer follows a second one: what data pairs and what protocol do we need to build the next generation of games? Recent work often uses video models as "renderers" that turn engine frames into final frames. But for rendering alone, image models such as DLSS 5 are the better fit: more stable, real-time, and free of long-term memory problems. What a video model adds over an image model is generation along time. In a game, that means animation detail and semantically fine-grained interaction, and that is where it should be used. AAA games ship with enormous libraries of hand-authored animation. GTA 6 has cost more than $2 billion and contains over 600,000 unique animations. That is a vast market. For stability and control, though, the video model should not generate the whole world. A lightweight game engine handles state and computes and stores every number. The engine also sets the camera and the protagonist's movement and passes them to the video model as a proxy video, which keeps the output controllable. With today's technology, a sensible split looks like this. The engine provides a coarse white-box clip: character A hits character B with a ranged attack for 80 damage, with no detailed motion. From the player's character sheet, the video model turns that "ranged attack" into something concrete. It can be a fireball, with the casting motion and fire effects, or a thunder hammer, with the swing and the lightning. However it looks, the hit timing and the 80 damage stay exactly as the engine computed them. Everyone plays the same engine, but each player gets their own game. 🌐 Project: https://game-world-model.github.io/

title: Let the Fixer Decide: Training a Code Localizer from the Fixer's Likelihood

details.title: Let the Fixer Decide: Training a Code Localizer from the Fixer's Likelihood
details.abstract: Code localizers are usually trained to predict the files a reference patch edits, but the code a fixer needs to read is not the same as the code it changes. We propose Fixer-Guided Localization (FGL): the localizer proposes several localizations, a frozen fixer scores each by how likely it makes a verified patch, and the localizer is trained on these scores with weighted supervised fine-tuning, without running tests and without reinforcement learning. We build the full pipeline on Gemma 4 E4B for the Kaggle Gemma-4 Developer Agent competition, from 1,629 test-verified Kimi K3 trajectories. The FGL target helps the fixer find the bug as often as the teacher's localization while using 27.5% less code. On the development set, one EM round moves the agent in the expected direction compared with a matched control: more tasks reach a patch (53 vs. 46), fewer tasks get stuck reading files that do not exist (43 vs. 54), and more tasks are solved (8 vs. 6). Training also changes how the agent works: trained agents explore about three times more than the base model and write far fewer wrong patches, and the single agent solves up to 11 of 78 tasks, against 8 for the base model. An analysis of 13 evaluation runs identifies what limits a 4B agent under an 8-minute budget (time, repetition loops and edit quality) and gives practical lessons for training small coding agents. All data, code and adapters are publicly available.

title: ViDecide: Teaching Video Diffusion Models to Reason and Plan Step by Step

details.title: ViDecide: Teaching Video Diffusion Models to Reason and Plan Step by Step
details.abstract: We release ViDecide: Teaching video diffusion models to reason and plan step by step , which explores whether video diffusion models can reason and plan step by step, like the way language models do. Current video models often break physical or logical rules in multi-step reasoning and planning, even when the final frame looks right. We trace this to the conventional training paradigm, which generates a solution as one fixed-length clip instead of a chain of decisions. ViDecide makes three changes: 🧩 Causal generation with adaptive termination : the model generates one state transition at a time and decides when to stop with a visual EOS frame. 🎯 Decision-focused training schedule : training focuses on high noise levels, where the next move is decided. 🔁 Corrective Fine-tuning (CFT) : a new post-training method for autoregressive video diffusion. It maps the noise of a failed decision to the model's own successful continuation, avoiding the inaccurate credit assignment and unstable policy gradients of diffusion RL. On rule-based games (VideoRLVR), multi-step planning tasks (VBVR), and our new robot benchmark RoboTwin-Plan, ViDecide reaches an average strict success rate of 83.8% , vs. 23.3% for standard fine-tuning and 67.8% for the strongest prior method, and generalizes to larger puzzles and unseen layouts. Code, models, and data are open-sourced: 📄 Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26389 🌐 Project page: https://kevin-thu.github.io/ViDecide 💻 Code: https://github.com/Kevin-thu/ViDecide A ⭐ or an upvote would mean a lot, and we'd love to hear your thoughts! 🙏

details.title: AutoPILOT: A Visual Agent Harness for Real-Time Gameplay
details.abstract: This paper identifies a largely overlooked bottleneck in real-time visual agents: conventional harnesses execute only one action per model call, forcing agents to act slowly on stale observations. AutoPILOT allows models to delegate execution to open-loop macros or model-written closed-loop visual controllers, and introduces AFK-Bench, a benchmark of 120 games that continue running during inference. Without changing the underlying model, AutoPILOT improves GPT-6.1 Sol’s real-time success rate from 38.3% to 68.6% over VISTA while reducing cost, showing that how model outputs are executed over time is a central dimension of agent design.

title: Open Vision Banana: An Open Framework for Unified Visual Perception through Generation in RGB Space

details.title: Open Vision Banana: An Open Framework for Unified Visual Perception through Generation in RGB Space
details.abstract: Vision Banana showed that a closed image generator, instruction-tuned to paint perception outputs as RGB images, becomes a generalist vision model. Does this carry over to \emph{open} generators, and if not, what fails? We answer with \textbf{Open Vision Banana (OVB)}, an open framework that adapts the 7B diffusion generator of Qwen-Image-2.1 into one instruction-driven model for metric depth, semantic, instance, and referring segmentation, using a single shared low-rank adapter and public data. Each task is a \emph{task contract} whose RGB encoder, instruction, and decoder share one specification and are checked before training. Studying 42 externally evaluated checkpoints from two 100k-update runs, six exact weight-space merges, and eight controlled shorter runs, we find that the gap to the closed system is specific and measurable. Geometry is learned early while absolute scale is not: median-aligned NYUv2 δ1 stays at 0.89--0.93 throughout training as unaligned δ1 wanders between 0.11 and 0.50. The scale is not committed by a single sample: a ten-seed ensemble lifts unaligned δ1 from 0.348 to 0.516 without retraining. Depth and 2D segmentation compete for the shared adapter, and weight merging moves along this trade-off without escaping it. Finally, lower validation flow loss comes with lower Cityscapes accuracy (Spearman ρ≈−0.9 between loss reduction and mIoU), so the loss cannot select checkpoints. We release code, contracts, training data, and all evaluation outputs.

title: GameAnything: From Any Inspirations to Playable Game Worlds

details.title: GameAnything: From Any Inspirations to Playable Game Worlds
details.abstract: GameAnything: From Any Inspirations to Playable Game Worlds AI-driven game development holds the potential to transform diverse human inspirations into interactive experiences. However, existing systems and benchmarks primarily focus on explicit development specifications, with limited support for adapting multimodal references and evaluating actual gameplay experiences. We introduce GameAnything , an open-source agentic platform that transforms multimodal inspirations into playable extensions of existing games through iterative development. GameAnything integrates coding agents with an independent playtesting critic, persistent development state, and reusable experience memory to support continuous refinement. We further present GameAnything-Bench , a benchmark spanning diverse reference modalities, game creation objectives, and gaming environments, with exploratory gameplay testing to assess both functional correctness and gameplay quality. Evaluations of nine coding agent configurations reveal that current agents can adapt reference content but still struggle with playable interactions and precise modifications. Moreover, multimodal references improve content fidelity, while iterative refinement yields substantial but varying improvements across agents. These findings highlight both the potential and remaining challenges of inspiration-driven game development.

title: HIVE-Bench: Evaluating Patch-Level Visual Representations for Egocentric Robot Manipulation

details.title: HIVE-Bench: Evaluating Patch-Level Visual Representations for Egocentric Robot Manipulation
details.abstract: Pretrained vision is a common start for robot learning, but most comparisons still score one pooled vector from a third-person image. Bimanual policies instead read dense patch tokens from cameras on the robot. We introduce HIVE-Bench: one shared flow-matching policy reads 20 encoders from seven families on 24 egocentric bimanual tasks, across adaptation, task sharing, and sweeps of data, model size, and layer. Keeping the patches matters. Averaging each view to one token removes most of the success, adaptation helps every pair we test, and one shared policy keeps most of the success of separate policies at a fraction of the updates. The same tokens are then scored with statistics, state and object readouts, published vision scores, and an inverse-dynamics readout. That readout of the commanded motion is one of the strongest measurements available before a policy is trained. Recognition, depth, and correspondence do not transfer reliably. Fine-tuning can improve the action readout even when other measurements move the other way, and no statistic is stable enough to replace a rollout before any deployment.

title: Self-WSP: Can Language Models Improve Themselves Through Weight-Space Programming?

details.title: Self-WSP: Can Language Models Improve Themselves Through Weight-Space Programming?
details.abstract: Can a language model improve itself by editing its own weights? We explore this with a 0.8B model, achieving substantial gains on GSM8K (11.8% → 62.2%) and MATH500 (7.0% → 32.2%), while finding that the model often fails to understand what its edits actually do, and that random search can also yield meaningful improvements.

title: Can Latent Reasoning Drive LLM Outputs Without a Trace?

details.title: Can Latent Reasoning Drive LLM Outputs Without a Trace?
details.abstract: Can an LLM pursue a complex hidden objective by reasoning only in its hidden states, with no trace in its output? We show that it can. Deeper latent reasoning. We train with a linear "step predictor" that reads each intermediate step from the hidden states. Models reach at least 5x more latent steps at the same training budget. Hidden objectives in realistic tasks. In loan decisions and in C code, the fine-tuned model (Qwen3.5 9B) follows a hidden objective that takes 5 steps to compute. Its reasoning justifies the output without a word about the hidden objective, and a strong LLM monitor does not flag it. Not just easy. Told in its prompt what to compute, the untuned model either works it out in its reasoning and gets caught, or answers directly and is at chance. Mechanism. Activation patching shows that the model runs the hidden computation at the input tokens, step by step across its layers, before it generates any reasoning. Takeaway: monitoring should not rely on a model's output alone. Project page, with an interactive walkthrough: https://tomerashuach.github.io/clr/

title: Embodied-Harness: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Robotic Manipulation

details.title: Embodied-Harness: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Robotic Manipulation
details.abstract: Can a robot improve across attempts while its model parameters stay frozen? In Embodied-Harness , we explore recursive self-improvement (RSI) for robotic manipulation. The Actor follows operational guidance to carry out a task. After a failed attempt, the Reflector uses the execution trace and prior experience to diagnose what went wrong and revise that guidance. The Actor then tries again with the revised guidance, and the new execution trace informs the next round of reflection. Embodied-Harness achieves success rates of 82.4% on RoboTwin 2.0 , 76.7% on RoboSPA , and 94.4% on RMBench . On three real-world manipulation tasks, it achieves an average success rate of 96.7% .

title: A Pipeline-Parallel System for Depth-Recurrent Models

details.title: A Pipeline-Parallel System for Depth-Recurrent Models
details.abstract: Depth-recurrent (Looped) models raise effective depth by applying a shared stack of blocks several times. Scaling them usually requires pipeline parallelism, but commonly used interleaved 1F1B is drawn for an acyclic stage graph in which each micro-batch enters each stage once. Once that stack is split across stages, the same stage is visited several times on one micro-batch and later stages feed earlier ones: native 1F1B has no slot for the extra visit, cannot rank a first iteration against a second, and its neighbour-only send/receive order has no back edge to the first stage, so the arrangement stalls or fires out of order. We present Loop-PP, which rebuilds both the timetable and the communication for this cyclic layout. It schedules different iterations of the same stage separately, specializes a 1F1B skeleton into a globally consistent order over those visits, and emits a static instruction stream per rank that separates posting from waiting so communication overlaps local compute. Loop-PP is bit-identical to a single-stage reference. On 8B-60B MoE models, it lowers peak memory by as much as 32.8%, and with compute budget fixed, the best observed throughput rises by 12.7%.

title: MomentMem: Memorizing Key Moments for Robot Manipulation

details.title: MomentMem: Memorizing Key Moments for Robot Manipulation
details.abstract: 🤔 After picking up a block, can a robot still remember where it was originally placed? Is robot memory only about tracking task progress? Excited to share our recent work MomentMem: Memorizing Key Moments for Robot Manipulation ! ✨ Our goal is to enable robots to remember fleeting but critical visual observations and use them to guide future actions. 🔍 Motivation In many manipulation tasks, the information needed for future actions lies in what the robot saw earlier but can no longer observe. Storing the entire observation history introduces substantial redundancy, while textual summaries may lose precise spatial information and subtle visual details. We study Visual Moment Memory : how can robots capture critical visual details at the right moment and retrieve them when needed for subsequent actions? 🎯 Key Contributions Visual Moment Memory: We highlight a memory challenge beyond task progress tracking. Some transient visual details are unrelated to task progress yet crucial to successful manipulation. VMBench: A benchmark specifically designed to evaluate visual memory in robot manipulation, featuring 9 tasks with 100 successful demonstrations per task, covering spatial information, visual appearance, and their associations. MomentMem: A "keyframe album" for robots. A VLM identifies which observations are worth remembering, while a VLA leverages the stored original images for action execution, preserving fine-grained visual information. 📊 Key Findings Remembering key moments matters: MomentMem achieves an average success rate of 49.9% on VMBench, compared to just 7% without memory. Learning to remember reduces annotation requirements for new tasks: After training on other tasks, MomentMem adapts to Flash Beacon using only 5 memory-annotated demonstrations, achieving a success rate of 43.7%, comparable to 44.3% with full memory supervision. Both settings use 100 target-task action demonstrations to train the action execution module. Memory also helps in the real world: Compared with π0.5, MomentMem improves the number of successful trials from 3/30 to 14/30 in returning a block to its demonstrated location, and from 11/30 to 17/30 in finding a block under cups. 💡 Remembering key visual moments is one step toward enabling robots to leverage past experiences. How robots can make better use of the rich visual details in their memories remains an exciting direction for future research. We would love to hear your thoughts and discuss memory mechanisms for robot manipulation! 📄 Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26745

title: Wactorz: Self-Writing LLM Agents That Discover, Repair, and Migrate at the Edge

details.title: Wactorz: Self-Writing LLM Agents That Discover, Repair, and Migrate at the Edge
details.abstract: Most LLM agent frameworks run a task and exit. Wactorz is an open-source runtime in which LLM-written agents are long-lived, supervised actors: a planner turns a chat request into Python and compiles it into a new actor at runtime, and a supervisor restarts that actor alone, with its state intact, when it crashes. All coordination runs over MQTT, so agents can be spawned on, and live-migrated between, edge nodes such as a Raspberry Pi. In the demo, one chat request builds a camera-to-lamp automation. A second agent with a deliberate division-by-zero repairs its own code without losing its count, then live-migrates to a freshly deployed Raspberry Pi, in under four minutes and for $0.13 of model usage. This is the extended version of our AAAI-27 demo paper. It also covers the Wiring view of the topic graph, using Wactorz as a library for hand-written agents, how trained models are stored and sent to nodes, the security model and the limitations. Code is Apache 2.0, and feedback is very welcome!

title: NoHairCache: Calibrate-Once KV Cache Eviction with One Power-Law Exponent

details.title: NoHairCache: Calibrate-Once KV Cache Eviction with One Power-Law Exponent
details.abstract: The decay exponent α in KV-cache eviction is an intrinsic property of the model: calibrated once on a single corpus, it transfers directly across domains. Attention-based accumulation (H2O) and recency-based sliding windows (StreamingLLM) are two dominant eviction frameworks, often treated as unrelated, but we show that they are the two endpoints of a single power-law family: by scoring each token as si=Ai⋅(t−i)−α, where Ai is cumulative attention and α controls the age penalty, H2O and StreamingLLM correspond to α=0 and α→∞, respectively (with StreamingLLM additionally hard-coding an attention-sink patch). The no-hair mechanism of \citet{xiang2026nohair} bounds the admissible range of α, and the measured exponents agree: calibrating once on WikiText yields [0.556,0.822] for a representative model (Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct). The per-model ranges are consistent across five models (410M--1.5B) and independently match the optimal regions from perplexity sweeps. \textsc{NoHairCache} achieves the lowest perplexity across three datasets (WikiText, PG19, and arXiv) without per-dataset tuning, outperforming both H2O and StreamingLLM (p<0.05 on all three datasets, with 0.06--0.10 PPL gains over StreamingLLM at budget 512). On downstream four-way multiple-choice QA, it matches or outperforms StreamingLLM across all nine (task, budget) cells, retaining 98.2% of full-cache accuracy on NarrativeQA at 25% retention versus 91.1% for StreamingLLM; per-cell McNemar tests are not significant, so QA is corroborating only. We release our calibration script and drop-in scorer upon publication.

title: Innata-0: A Native Embodied World System with Model-Agent Co-Design

details.title: Innata-0: A Native Embodied World System with Model-Agent Co-Design
details.abstract: The physical world is open-ended, dynamic, and partially observable. While foundation models have advanced embodied intelligence, standalone models struggle with long-horizon execution, and simply integrating models with agents may lead to inconsistencies between planning and physical control. To support reliable and adaptive behaviors in the physical world, we introduce Innata-0, a native embodied world system. Innata-0 jointly designs an embodied world-action model and an agent to combine their complementary strengths. The model, Innata-0-WAM, adopts a tri-tower Mixture-of-Transformers architecture that integrates understanding, prediction, and action generation. The agent, Innata-0-Agent, coordinates long-horizon execution through memory, verification, and recovery. A co-design protocol is further proposed to align model training with agent execution and leverage validated experiences to support subsequent adaptation and model improvement. Extensive evaluations demonstrate strong embodied capabilities across understanding, world prediction, and robotic manipulation. Innata-0 represents our first step toward physical intelligence, and we see it as the beginning of a much longer journey.

title: LLMs Memorize Their Own Hallucinations During Post-Training

details.title: LLMs Memorize Their Own Hallucinations During Post-Training
details.abstract: Reasoning-centric post-training recipes (outcome-based RL rewards) are now applied well beyond math and code. We show that on knowledge tasks, these recipes cause models to memorize the hallucinations they generate in their own reasoning chains. By defining a memorization score, we show that: Recall of self-generated hallucinations that get rewarded during RL rises by 4.83% on average, vs. just 0.17% for hallucinations that receive no training signal. Models even memorize false facts they immediately retract in their reasoning ("No wait, that can't be right..."). Memorization is strongest on the hardest training questions, and rewarding a hallucination makes models less likely to abstain from it later (by 7.23% on average).

title: WeaveVLA: 3D Relational Grounding for Vision-Language-Action Models

details.title: WeaveVLA: 3D Relational Grounding for Vision-Language-Action Models
details.abstract: WeaveVLA: Enhancing Robotic Spatial Intelligence through 3D Relational Grounding Recent advances in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have accelerated the development of embodied intelligence. Despite their growing 3D spatial awareness, existing VLA models still face challenges in localizing task-relevant objects and modeling their relative spatial relationships. Moreover, different stages of manipulation involve different spatial relationships, which continuously evolve during execution. Selectively modeling task-relevant spatial relationships and capturing their temporal evolution remain important challenges for robust robotic manipulation. To address these challenges, we introduce WeaveVLA: 3D Relational Grounding for Vision-Language-Action Models , a framework that integrates explicit 3D spatial relationships and temporal relational memory into VLA models. WeaveVLA constructs a task-conditioned sparse 3D spatial graph to explicitly represent key spatial relationships. By combining Graph Transformers with Recurrent Edge Updates, it continuously integrates current geometric information with historical relational context. The resulting graph representations are summarized into compact Relational Tokens, which complement the original vision-language features to guide robot action generation, bringing together spatial perception, relational memory, and robotic control. We validate the effectiveness of WeaveVLA on two VLA backbones: StarVLA-GR00T and π₀.₅. LIBERO: Average success rates reach 98.3% and 98.2%, respectively. LIBERO-Plus: Success rates improve from 74.9% to 82.0% and from 85.7% to 87.8%, respectively. CALVIN: The average completed task sequence length reaches 3.997. Real-world dual-arm manipulation: The average success rate improves from 55.6% to 70.0% under standard conditions, and from 33.3% to 53.3% under out-of-distribution (OOD) perturbations. By integrating explicit 3D spatial relationships and temporal relational memory into VLA models, WeaveVLA offers a new approach to enhancing robotic spatial intelligence, generalization, and manipulation robustness.

title: Deterministic, Reproducible Inference in Exact Integer Arithmetic, and Verifiable Distributed Inference as Its Consequence

details.title: Deterministic, Reproducible Inference in Exact Integer Arithmetic, and Verifiable Distributed Inference as Its Consequence
details.abstract: We present tritify, an open-source runtime that runs the forward pass of real models — decoder-only LLMs, MoE decoders, and the SAM 2.1 image/video stack — entirely in exact integer arithmetic, with floating point confined to offline quantization. The output is bit-identical across hardware and across CPU/GPU, reproduces the float reference's decisions with the numeric exceptions measured, and stays byte-identical when the model is split across machines. That last point is the payoff: verifiable distributed inference — an untrusted server or a fleet of devices runs the model while an open scalar oracle re-derives the exact bytes. title: How Complete Must an Environment Be to Train a Capable GUI Agent?

details.title: How Complete Must an Environment Be to Train a Capable GUI Agent?
details.abstract: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents are widely trained in executable GUI environments. To lower cost, build environments in batches, and reduce manual effort, each work trades away part of the environment through its construction choices. We describe these choices along three dimensions: reward coverage, the goal-reaching trajectories the verifier rewards; data coverage, the application data the agent is exposed to beyond what the task reads or writes; and feature coverage, the application features beyond what the task uses. Existing works set each dimension on engineering grounds, but they do not measure its effect on training. How complete must an environment be to train a capable agent, and along which dimensions? In MobileGym, we adjust each dimension separately, train Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct, and evaluate every policy in the original full environment. A verifier that rewards only one reference path lowers success by 10.53 points, and removing unneeded records also lowers success. Pruning unneeded features instead raises success from 51.61% to 56.13%, entirely on tasks whose environments it left unchanged. The gain reverses when each episode is weighted equally and vanishes when only episodes on the pruned tasks are balanced. Without pruning, length weighting there reinforces long detour successes that erode skills on other tasks. Following these findings, we build MobileGym-Lite, which keeps reward and data coverage complete and prunes unneeded features. It outperforms Full in the full environment (55.48% versus 51.61% success) with lower construction cost.

title: Beyond Attention Maps: Understanding and Improving Medical MLLMs via Visual Values

details.title: Beyond Attention Maps: Understanding and Improving Medical MLLMs via Visual Values
details.abstract: Are We Overlooking the V in MLLMs Attention? Most existing studies on MLLMs focus on improving spatial attention — teaching models where to look. But does looking at the right region necessarily lead to a correct answer? In our recent work, Beyond Attention Maps: Understanding and Improving Medical MLLMs via Visual Values, we revisit this question using paired non-contrast and contrast-enhanced medical images. Our findings reveal that: 🔹 Highly similar attention maps can lead to drastically different predictions. 🔹 Intervening on visual values (V) produces substantially larger prediction changes than intervening on attention weights. 🔹 Informative visual values remain beneficial even when attention maps are heavily perturbed. Motivated by these observations, we propose VIVID, a visual value-guided on-policy distillation framework that uses the student's response to enhanced visual evidence to refine teacher supervision. Beyond medical imaging, we hope to inspire a broader discussion: Should we shift some of our attention from learning where to look towards learning what to retrieve? And for on-policy distillation, should we focus not only on what the teacher predicts, but also on how visual evidence shapes its supervision? 📄 Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29361 🌐 Project: https://qiuzyc.github.io/VIVID We welcome discussions and feedback from the community! #MLLM #VisualUnderstanding #Attention #OnPolicyDistillation #MedicalAI

title: Lazy Agents Answer Against Their Own Beliefs: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Beliefs Teaches Them to Act on What They Believe

details.title: Lazy Agents Answer Against Their Own Beliefs: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Beliefs Teaches Them to Act on What They Believe
details.abstract: Lazy agents answer against their own beliefs. VLM agents on long tasks often commit to an answer while their own stated belief still names several possible answers, for example writing "Possible: cups 2, 4" and then answering cup 4. RLVB (Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Beliefs) moves agentic RL from verifiable rewards to verifiable beliefs. During training, the simulator knows the rules linking the hidden answer to the evidence, so it computes the exact posterior after every step. At each history, RLVB samples several turns and scores each action against a teacher that acts on this posterior: further steps are rewarded while the evidence still allows several answers, and an answer is rewarded once the evidence is sufficient. It needs no judge, critic or reward model. Across three VLMs and three benchmarks, two of which are never seen in training, RLVB improves the base model in all nine settings, by 17.1% on average. It outperforms PPO with a process reward from an LLM judge by 9.3% on average while using 1.6x fewer GPU-hours. With the outcome reward, GRPO and PPO fall below the base model on average. title: Rewirable Circuits in Transformers with Loom Attention

details.title: Rewirable Circuits in Transformers with Loom Attention
details.abstract: Hi everyone! Author here — happy to share LoomFormer , along with our JAX/Pallas training code, PyTorch/Triton inference kernels, and 300B-token 2.8B checkpoints (including a matched mHC-Pythia-2.8B baseline). TL;DR: Why layer-wise residual routing hits a ceiling: Recent residual-stream mechanisms ( HC/mHC , AttnRes , MUDDFormer ) share routing ports across all heads of a layer, restricting their head-to-head wiring matrix to rank ≤ 1 (or ≤ 3 in MUDDFormer). Per-token head-to-head rewiring: LoomFormer generates ports per head and per token via normalized and gated linear attention ( MRead / MWrite ) over a fixed per-token matrix memory M_t of shape [d_k, d] , reaching wiring rank 2n in a smaller per-token state ( 3D ) than 4-stream HC/mHC ( 4D ). Scaling & 300B pretraining: Matches Transformers trained with >3× compute across scales. Trained on 300B Pile tokens with only +1.95% FLOPs , LoomPythia-2.8B achieves 1.6× the downstream gain of mHC-Pythia-2.8B , matches Pythia-12B in 0-shot ( 59.9 ), and surpasses Pythia-12B in 5-shot ( 61.6 vs. 60.8 ) and FLAN ppl ( 6.94 vs. 7.26 ), while lifting deep non-sink active heads from ~20% to 74.4% . Wall-clock speed: Sustains 89–92% of Transformer training speed on TPU v5p (fused Pallas kernels) and 84–92% of prefill/decode speed on GPU (fused Triton + CUDA graphs). title: ACAP: Asynchronous Coding Agents for Efficient Robot Control

details.title: ACAP: Asynchronous Coding Agents for Efficient Robot Control
details.abstract: We are introducing ACAP: Asynchronous Coding Agents as Policy . A robot policy built from persistent coding agents that reason and act asynchronously. A single coding agent can issue parallel motion commands, but every decision still passes through one reasoning process. While it diagnoses a grasp with one arm, independent work on the other may wait. ACAP distributes decision-making across parts of one robot, with a hyper-agent coordinating their work. 🦾 Each member is a robot policy. A persistent agent controls a configurable group, such as an arm with its gripper or the torso and chassis. It observes, reasons, writes control code, acts and uses feedback to decide its next step. Members' reasoning and execution can overlap. 🧭 Let an agent coordinate the policies. The hyper-agent decides what to delegate, when members synchronize, and when the lead should directly control several parts. Members prepare flowers in parallel and take turns at the vase. For a shared towel fold, the lead controls both arms. Coordination comes from observations and feedback, without a hand-written script. ⚡ Lower time cost on real robots. Across 72 rollouts in 25 task/platform settings on Galaxea R1 Pro and AgileX PiPER-family robots, ACAP cuts task-balanced time cost by 28.2% versus a single-agent Direct Policy. It also has lower mean time cost than Fixed Delegation, where control always stays with members, on all eight collaborative settings, and than Direct on all six tasks of a separate 90-rollout repeated study. 🧮 From observations to geometry to action. Frontier coding agents control the robot through geometry they compute in code while the task is running. They model the scene, derive a motion, act and check how the object responds. An agent triangulates a thin flower tip by moving its hand, turns a fitted bottle axis into a corrective wrist rotation, and tracks carton features to overturn a mistaken slip diagnosis. 📦 162 real-world rollouts for research. The dataset preserves this behavior, linking observations, generated programs, numerical results, agent messages, actions and robot feedback. Researchers can trace how agents build representations, turn calculations into commands, and revise decisions from physical evidence. 📄 Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.31205 🌐 Project page: https://projects.zxhezexin.com/acap 🤗 Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/zxhezexin/acap-rollout-dataset We'd love to hear your thoughts. details.title: S-Mind: Internalizing Multi-View Geometry for Spatial Intelligence
details.abstract: Spatial intelligence, the ability to reason about 3D space from visual observations, becomes essential as multimodal large language models (MLLMs) move into the physical world. Beyond perceiving each view, it rests on two cornerstones of human cognition: fusing multiple views into one coherent 3D scene and mentally transforming that scene to new viewpoints as reasoning unfolds. Yet our spatial probes reveal that MLLMs largely lack both capabilities, even after spatial fine-tuning. We therefore present S-Mind, which internalizes multi-view geometry within the MLLM through a compact set of spatial tokens. It supervises these tokens to hold the fused 3D scene and re-emits them to re-express this scene from every viewpoint the reasoning adopts. (ii) Observation-Driven Closed-Loop Partition Refinement observes the current partition and its supporting evidence to select targeted inspection, evidence repair, composition, or reselection actions. It verifies proposed changes and uses the updated state and action outcomes to guide subsequent decisions. On PartObjaverse-Tiny-WT, PartAgent achieves 68.41 mIoU, outperforming the strongest competing method by 8.53 points. Across 3DCoMPaT200, PartNeXt, PartNetE, and PartObjaverse-Tiny, PartAgent achieves the highest mIoU on each dataset, averaging 69.36 on the four datasets, 7.28 points above the highest mean among competing methods. details.title: PhyCoVE: Benchmarking Physical Counterfactual Video Editing across Diverse Material Dynamics

Make it heavier, and the splash should grow. A physical edit changes not only how a scene looks, but how it evolves afterward. We introduce PhyCoVE , a benchmark for physical counterfactual video editing across rigid, elastic, and fluid dynamics: 📊 533 cases on 110 source videos , each pairing a source video and a physical edit with a counterfactual target video 🧪 5 interaction patterns (rigid–rigid, rigid–elastic, rigid–fluid, elastic–fluid, elastic–elastic), in both simulated and real-recorded scenes ✂️ 3 edit types : remove an object (178), change a physical quantity (334), insert an object (21), with 63 edits taking effect at a later frame 📐 Counterfactual Fidelity (CF) : measures how much of the source-to-target physical change a generated video reproduces; it ranks models nearly as human preference does (Kendall τ = 0.90), while pixel metrics favor the unedited source Key findings on 7 models (MiniMax H3, Seedance 2.5, Wan 3.0, Kling 4.0, JoyAI, Kiwi-Edit, OmniWeaving): Even the best model reproduces only ~1/7 of the physical change (CF = 0.134): models change how a scene looks, but rarely how it evolves Parameter edits (mass, stiffness, density, flow rate) are essentially unsolved (top CF = 0.019) Premature execution : 44 of 63 later-frame removals happen before the requested frame 🌐 Project page: https://phycove.github.io/ 🤗 Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/ccmoony/PhyCoVE 💻 Code: https://github.com/Hammour-steak/PhyCoVE

title: Reinforcing Diffusion Models by Instantaneous Trajectory Distribution Matching

details.title: Reinforcing Diffusion Models by Instantaneous Trajectory Distribution Matching
details.abstract: Hi everyone! 👋 Excited to share our new work iTDM (Instantaneous Trajectory Distribution Matching) for reinforcing diffusion and flow-matching models! TL;DR: Existing forward diffusion RL methods (enabling fast deterministic ODE rollouts without trajectory backprop, e.g., DGPO, DiffusionNFT, AWM) essentially rely on signed Reward-Weighted Regression (RWR) centered at the policy velocity $v_\theta$. We show that subtracting a reward baseline in RWR implicitly assumes $v_\theta = v_q$ (the rollout behavior velocity)—an assumption violated under CFG rollouts, offline/off-policy updates, and imperfect self-consistency, causing baseline-induced gradient drift and coarse few-step rollout artifact fitting . How iTDM fixes this: By taking the infinitesimal step-size limit of Trajectory Distribution Matching (TDM) via the Gaussian posterior-score identity, iTDM yields an exact sample-level RL gradient anchored at the behavior velocity $v_q$— without training an extra reward-tilted score network. Tracking $v_q$ online with a lightweight auxiliary LoRA denoiser and regularizing toward the frozen reference guarantees exact baseline invariance at the auxiliary optimum, naturally unifying online and offline RL without drift or blurry artifacts. Key Highlights: ⚡ ~3× Faster & Collapse-Free Scaling: Reaches 0.75 nearly 3× faster than DGPO, DiffusionNFT, and AWM on GenEval2 (SD3.5-M), scaling smoothly to 0.87 without training collapse. 🎯 Unlocks Stable CFG-Guided Online & Offline RL: Leads CFG-guided online RL across compositional generation ( 0.97 GenEval), text rendering ( 0.96 OCR), and preference alignment ( 24.08 PickScore) on SD3.5-M, while overcoming offline collapse/divergence under frozen rollouts ( 0.87 GenEval, 0.92 OCR, 22.26 PickScore; outperforming Diffusion-DPO across all tasks at $G=2$)—preserving/improving 7 unseen DrawBench metrics without background collapse or blurry textures. 🚀 Scales to 5.6B FLUX.3 Klein Base: Guidance-free ( CFG=1.0 ) reinforcement with HPSv3++ surpasses even the CFG-guided base model ( CFG=3.5 ) across both in-domain and unseen quality/alignment metrics. 🔗 Links: 🌐 Project Page: https://luo-yihong.github.io/iTDM/ 💻 Code: https://github.com/Luo-Yihong/iTDM 📄 Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30986

title: Coding4Games: Can Modern Coding Agents Play Modern Video Games?

details.title: Coding4Games: Can Modern Coding Agents Play Modern Video Games?
details.abstract: Games, especially modern AAA games, challenge language models to perceive complex scenes, control actions, and make decisions over long horizons. Existing game benchmarks primarily test language models as computer-use agents that query a language model throughout play, incurring repeated inference cost and, in real-time games, acting while the environment continues to evolve. We ask whether coding agents can learn from game interaction to develop standalone game-playing programs that run without language-model inference. We thus introduce Coding4Games, a benchmark for evaluating whether coding agents can develop standalone programs that play modern games through visual observations and standard game inputs. Coding4Games has three defining features: 1) Diverse Modern Games, covering 15 games with diverse visual, strategic, and control demands; 2) Development–Test Separation, in which a coding agent uses a sandbox and the standard player interface to iteratively develop a program, after which the selected program is frozen and independently tested without language-model inference; and 3) Outcome and Process Evaluation, which measures not only game performance and reliability but also how agents use feedback, revise programs, and resolve problems during development. Across 15 games, the best program per game outscores the strongest GUI baseline on 13 and ties it on one. The human player outscores all agents on 10 games. We additionally examine the effects of development budgets. Coding4Games evaluates whether coding agents can turn their understanding of complex interactive environments into programs that work reliably on their own.

title: Separating Measurement Failures from Defence Failures in Split Language-Model Privacy

details.title: Separating Measurement Failures from Defence Failures in Split Language-Model Privacy
details.abstract: Split-training privacy evaluations fail through distinct mechanisms. Evaluators can overlook an exposed gradient channel, align reconstructions against shifted labels, or deploy uncalibrated probes before testing a candidate defence, while calibrated attacks can also refute real defences. Separating these failure modes alters which claims survive. We conduct a retrospective evidentiary reanalysis across four split-LLM campaigns and two cross-cutting scope checks covering host key custody and variational mutual-information bounds, mapping every recorded claim to one of five admissibility states (breach, non-detection, undetermined coverage, invalid measurement, or out-of-scope inference). Across a 19-configuration exploration, only four of 24 required probes qualified, yet those four calibrated probes still established qualified privacy breaches in 13 configurations, while utility or learning-gain failures eliminated the remaining 6. In a seven-cell defence-redesign pilot, 2 quantised configurations failed utility gates, calibrated next-byte structure probes breached the 0.02 gate on all 7 cells (0.097 to 0.112), and qualified punctuation-property probes reached 0.79 to 0.89, yielding 4 failed and 3 undetermined composite privacy assessments (the latter from marginal null-band excursions on punctuation bindings). Negative evidence against both defence families remains intact. Scope checks further show that shared-key orthogonal wrappers protect passive network captures without hiding activations from a compromised restoring host, and why near-zero variational lower bounds leave worst-case leakage unconstrained. Rerunnable scripts verify 1,522 checks across 122 SHA-256-pinned artifacts while preserving each campaign's native seed intervals and retrospective boundaries.

title: AdProducer: Towards Agentic Advertising Video Generation

details.title: AdProducer: Towards Agentic Advertising Video Generation
details.abstract: Recent advances in video generation have made automated advertising production increasingly feasible. However, an effective advertisement must faithfully represent the product and communicate its selling points through compelling visual storytelling, which requires more than visual synthesis: it calls for deeper product understanding and strategic decisions about how to present product value. Crucially, product research and creative design are closely intertwined, as the information gathered about a product determines which features can be faithfully demonstrated and how they should be presented. In this paper, we introduce AdProducer, the first end-to-end agentic framework for advertising video creation, transforming concise creative briefs into finished advertisements. Our multimodal agent autonomously researches products through web and image search and translates its findings into selling-point-driven storyboards that guide a frozen video generator. To achieve this, we develop a dedicated data construction pipeline that yields two training datasets, AdProducer-SFT and AdProducer-RL, and train the agent through supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning with joint optimization of storyboard- and video-level rewards. We further introduce AdCreation-Bench, comprising 305 advertising briefs across eight domains, with two complementary metrics: PG-Score for product correctness and creative execution, and Ad-Score for overall advertising effectiveness assessed by an independent judge. Experiments demonstrate that AdProducer improves the PG-Score of MiniMax H3 from 17.3 to 51.3 and generalizes to Veo 3.1 without additional training, improving its score from 28.0 to 35.9, with consistent gains in Ad-Score, VideoScore2, and human evaluations. details.title: Do learned image captioning metrics generalize? Auditing duplicated samples in human-judgment benchmarks
details.abstract: Hi everyone! We're excited to share our recent work: Do Learned Image Captioning Metrics Generalize? Auditing Duplicated Samples in Human-Judgment Benchmarks How reliable are the reported gains of learned image captioning metrics? To find out, we conducted a systematic audit of three recent human-judgment benchmarks: Polaris , Nebula , and Spica . Key Findings: Substantial Data Leakage: 68.4% of the Polaris test set appears verbatim in the Spica training set (identical images, captions, and human ratings). Memorization Over Generalization: Over five training epochs, Pearl's gain on duplicated samples jumps from 2.5 to 10.4 Kendall's τ points, while performance on non-duplicated samples remains virtually flat. Flawed Evaluation Signals: Much of the reported correlation is driven by spotting the lowest-rated captions, which masks differences in fine-grained ranking ability. Rethinking the Leaderboard: Under a leakage-controlled protocol, zero-shot VLM judges take the lead, while a simple ridge regression on frozen features matches or outperforms several complex learned metrics. To address these issues, we propose a more rigorous evaluation protocol, with broader implications for evaluators trained on human judgments. Resources & Reproducibility: 📄 Paper: arXiv:2611.30488 💻 Code & Tools: GitHub Repo (deduplication tools and reproduction scripts) 🤗 Data & Checkpoints: Hugging Face Dataset (model weights, 82 retrained checkpoints, and per-sample scores) Note: All 23 tables and 300 reported numbers can be reproduced on CPU only—no expensive GPUs required.

title: Can an Agent Trust Its Own Zoom? Cross-Magnification Provenance Verification for Whole-Slide Images

details.title: Can an Agent Trust Its Own Zoom? Cross-Magnification Provenance Verification for Whole-Slide Images
details.abstract: Visual agents navigate whole-slide images through magnified observations associated with claimed locations. However, a visually plausible observation does not necessarily originate from its claimed location, particularly across magnifications and in regions with similar tissue structures. We formulate cross-magnification provenance verification (CMPV) to evaluate whether visual evidence supports a claimed spatial association, recover the source when possible, and abstain when evidence is insufficient. We introduce PyraFault, a benchmark of 3.06 million coordinate-supervised examples from 2,200 cases across five TCGA cohorts, covering within-context substitutions, absent-source faults, and geometric perturbations. We further propose ZoomTrace, a claim-independent verifier that estimates the observation's source before evaluating its agreement with the claimed location. It combines physical-scale alignment, visual retrieval, geometric refinement, and reliability estimation using spatially disjoint competing matches. On 503,320 test examples, ZoomTrace achieves 0.969 AUPRC and 0.987 AUROC, compared with 0.789 and 0.903 for Efficient LoFTR. Further evaluations reveal trade-offs in reliability estimation and limitations in vision-language models, cross-dataset retrieval, and calibration. Integrating ZoomTrace into visual agent tool paths reduces exposure to corrupted observations and silent failures, while downstream accuracy improvements depend on the agent and verification threshold.

details.title: Escriba-OCR: A 1B Vision-Language Model for Error-Preserving Transcription of Handwritten Portuguese Essays
details.abstract: Escriba-OCR-1B is a 1B-parameter OCR model that transcribes handwritten Brazilian Portuguese essays exactly as the student wrote them: misspellings, line breaks, struck-through words and insertions included. Feedback tools and research on learner writing need that, but vision-language models tend to rewrite the text into correct Portuguese. Benchmark. 22 open baselines (0.8B to 400B parameters) on the 199 BRESSAY test pages, scored on CER plus error preservation, invented errors, edit-markup precision and recall, and line structure, with paired bootstrap confidence intervals. Every VLM replaces 39–78% of the words that are not in a Portuguese dictionary with dictionary words. Model. LightOnOCR-3-1B fine-tuned on 647 pages in 85 minutes on one GPU: 2.06% CER against 5.60% for the best baseline, Qwen3-VL 235B-A22B (95% CI of the difference [−4.2, −2.9]). It recovers 77% of illegible deletions and 67% of insertions, and gets the line structure right on 97% of the pages. Runs at school. Quantised to 4 bits, it transcribes a page in about a minute on an ordinary CPU, so the essays never leave the school's computers. Limits. It still normalises 60% of likely misspellings, and on 40 letters from another corpus it misreads words it never saw in training more often than its base model. A teacher's review finds that 45% of the judgeable apparent corrections are errors in the BRESSAY ground truth. title: InstructReplay: Replaying Assistant Turns to Preserve General Behavior During Factual Fine-Tuning

details.title: InstructReplay: Replaying Assistant Turns to Preserve General Behavior During Factual Fine-Tuning
details.abstract: Fine-tuning an instruction-tuned language model on new facts often erodes its general abilities. We find that standard fine-tuning lowers instruction-following, reasoning and coding benchmarks by 35 points on average, and that these losses track a collapse in answer length: fine-tuned models at least halve their responses, and the further a response drifts from the initial model's length, the more often it fails. We propose InstructReplay: the initial model answers a set of general instructions once, and during fine-tuning the model is kept close to the initial model on these answers. Across three model families and two domains, InstructReplay reduces the average decline on five general benchmarks from 28.1 to 2.4 points and keeps answer length close to the initial model's, while learning the new facts as well as standard fine-tuning. It balances learning and retention better than seven adaptation methods in all six settings. Controlled comparisons attribute the gain to replaying the model's own answers to general instructions rather than to the form of the loss.

title: RECAP: Training Long-horizon LLM Agents with Context Compaction

details.title: RECAP: Training Long-horizon LLM Agents with Context Compaction
details.abstract: How can we train AI agents to solve long-horizon tasks with limited context? We introduce RECAP🎞️, an RL recipe for training long-horizon agents with context compaction. The central idea is simple: a good summary should preserve the agent’s behavior under the original interaction history. RECAP combines final task rewards with the measure of how compaction changes the agent's behavior. We evaluate RECAP on two environments and demonstrate consistent improvements over task-reward-only baselines: 🔎 BrowseComp-Plus: 58.2% → 62.8% (+4.6 pp) 🛠️ SWE-bench Verified: 46.8% → 51.1% (+4.3 pp) These gains come with fewer tool calls and shorter trajectories. title: Small Learned Projections for Semantic-Reversal-Aware Retrieval with Spectral Acceleration: A Four-Domain Empirical Study

details.title: Small Learned Projections for Semantic-Reversal-Aware Retrieval with Spectral Acceleration: A Four-Domain Empirical Study
details.abstract: Dense retrievers fail adversarially: swap a document A for a near-copy B that differs by one small meaning-changing edit (a "trap"), and raw cosine over E5-Large-v2 ranks the trap in the top-10 for 82–100% of queries at a 5,000-pool. We show a small learned projection W: R^1024 → R^d (d ∈ {11, 32}), trained by a deterministic recipe on a declared set of cases, suppresses it: for the declared cases HN@10 = 0.0000 (no trap in the top-10) in all twelve (domain, pool-size) settings across four independent domains — legal, medical, patent, financial — and pools up to 100,000, while the correct paraphrase is retained. A spectral accelerator serves the projected search 116–143× faster than exact scoring. Open method and a full reproducibility package — trap sets, lenses, trainer, and hashed results. title: ReFocus: Progress-Guided Adaptive Practice for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation Reinforcement Learning

details.title: ReFocus: Progress-Guided Adaptive Practice for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation Reinforcement Learning
details.abstract: Online reinforcement learning (RL) enables vision-language-action policies to improve through environmental interaction. However, in long-horizon manipulation, sparse success/failure feedback provides little information about where policies encounter bottlenecks. Moreover, repeated full-task rollouts also leave these bottlenecks weakly analyzed and insufficiently practiced. To this end, we introduce \textbf{ReFocus}, a progress-guided multi-round RL framework that alternates Global with Local RL to identify task-specific bottlenecks and allocate additional practice to them. Specifically, during Global RL, we decompose each task into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of subtasks. Then a DAG-based Progress Reward is leveraged for both policy training and bottleneck diagnosis. Based on the identified bottlenecks, ReFocus selects Adaptive Practice Windows, defining task segments from an entry stage to a target stage. It allocates additional interaction to these segments during Local RL while updating the entire policy. After that, it evaluates the policy to perform the full-task for the next round RL, forming an iteration between Global and Local RL. Experiments on LIBERO-Long and RoboCasa365 show that ReFocus achieves success rates of 97.8% and 51.3% respectively, compared with 90.6% and 39.3% for the $\pi_{0.5}$ baseline. Furthermore, we evaluate a real-world adaptation on three long-horizon tasks. On BreadBaker, ReFocus achieves 95% success, compared with 30% for the $\pi_{0.5}$.

title: Sage-Med: Scaling Medical Multimodal Intelligence

details.title: Sage-Med: Scaling Medical Multimodal Intelligence
details.abstract: Hi everyone! 👋 We are the Sage-Med Team , excited to share our paper: Sage-Med: Scaling Medical Multimodal Intelligence . TL;DR: We benchmarked 77 models across 238 clinical tasks (61 public + 13 private multi-center benchmarks from 14 hospitals and institutions, 40+ modalities) to diagnose why medical multimodal scaling stalls. Guided by these findings, we introduce Sage-Med-Preview (35B-A3B) , combining stage-specific six-step curation over 322.7M candidate records with medical pretraining, 3-stage progressive SFT, and adaptive GRPO reinforcement learning with difficulty sampling and independent reference replay. 🔍 Benchmarking Insights: The Visual Scaling Bottleneck Existing medical MLLMs still trail general-purpose MLLMs on 29 of 31 public multimodal benchmarks. Parameter scaling within a model family mainly improves text ( +9.90% text-only understanding, +12.37% text-only reasoning), while yielding much smaller gains on multimodal understanding ( +4.34% ). Enabling reasoning modes boosts text reasoning and knowledge, yet brings virtually no gain to visual perception ( 0.54% difference across 22 perception benchmarks) and can even weaken perception within the same backbone. 🚀 Model Performance & Preliminary Training Exploration Leading open-source multimodal performance: Achieves 58.26% across 31 public multimodal benchmarks (vs. 50.99% for Hulu-Med-235B-A22B and 52.24% for Intern-S2-Preview), 59.81% on 15 specialized benchmarks, and 80.05% on comprehensive multimodal understanding (ahead of GPT-6.2-Sol at 76.81%). Strong multi-center generalization: Ranks #1 overall on unseen private multi-center clinical benchmarks at 57.72% (vs. 51.24% for GPT-6.2-Sol). Preliminary pipeline ablations: We also share initial explorations and ablations on our training pipeline (pretraining data composition, base-model initialization, modality and response-length mixtures, and progressive SFT + adaptive RL), suggesting that supervision quality, modality balance, and curriculum design outweigh raw data volume alone. 🔗 Links: Website | Hugging Face | GitHub | Leaderboard We hope both the model and our empirical findings are useful to the community. Feel free to drop any questions on our data recipes, ablations, or evaluation!

title: Mixture-of-Loops Transformer

details.title: Mixture-of-Loops Transformer
details.abstract: Looped Transformers boost expressivity by reusing shared layers across loops, yet at the cost of efficiency. Pushing their expressivity-efficiency frontier requires rethinking the core mechanism connecting adjacent loops: What should be passed as a Transformer loops? We introduce Mixture-of-Loops Transformer (MoLT), whose Mixture-of-Loops Attention (MoLA) uses keys and values (KV) as memory for selective reuse across depths and loops. Under loop residual, MoLT-R retains the residual stream and reads local KV across loops for expressivity. Under loop KV, MoLT-KV instead restarts from embeddings and reads current-loop local KV with preceding-loop memory KV at earlier positions for efficiency. MoLT-KV eliminates same-position cross-loop dependence and, paired with loop forcing for parallel training, unlocks single-traversal Mixture-of-Loops (MoL) decoding beyond the training loop horizon. To balance efficiency and quality, we introduce U-shaped MoLT (U-MoLT), which separates memory construction from prediction readout and skips unused decoder traversals without changing predictions. In 400B-token pretraining, U-MoLT outperforms OLMo3 across 700M/1.5B dense and 3B MoE models, achieving 1.7x validation cross-entropy (CE) token efficiency at 700M while improving 3B MoE 10-domain perplexity by 0.75 and 10-task accuracy by 2.1 percentage points. In 100B-token continued pretraining of Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base, our U-MoLT adaptation lowers CE on all 11 domains over the matched baseline with 1.4x mean token efficiency. At inference, U-MoLT with MoL-Hybrid-2 matches non-looped OLMo3 latency at 996.6 vs. 1,000.6 ms on S-size (~113M) models. Code is available at this https URL

title: Playfulness as Feedback for Agentic Game Development

details.title: Playfulness as Feedback for Agentic Game Development
details.abstract: Coding agents can generate runnable games from natural-language descriptions. However, a runnable game does not guarantee an excellent gameplay experience for players. In our view, a playful game should provide 1) reliable core functionality, 2) appealing visual design and assets, and 3) rich gameplay that supports exploration and progression. How agents can improve these aspects of playfulness remains underexplored. In our work, we propose Play2Evolve, a recursive game development framework with three stages: Initialization, Refinement, and Evolution. Using playfulness as feedback, agents playtest the game and diagnose issues in its functionality, visual presentation, and gameplay. Their feedback guides bug fixes and asset improvements. It also helps agents propose new gameplay and aesthetic goals for continued game evolution. To enrich game materials, we combine a video generation model with code to create appealing static and dynamic assets and integrate them into interactive gameplay. Finally, Play2Evolve achieves state-of-the-art performance among the evaluated methods, scoring 60.05 on GameCraft-Bench compared with 50.81 after Game Initialization and 52.46 for Play2Code. Human overall-quality ratings reach 3.67, compared with 2.38 and 2.43, respectively. Our code will be released at this https URL.

title: EgoUseBench: Benchmarking Computer-Use Agents under Evolving First-Person Contexts

details.title: EgoUseBench: Benchmarking Computer-Use Agents under Evolving First-Person Contexts
details.abstract: AI wearables, such as smart glasses, extend the context available to agents beyond digital environments to users' everyday physical surroundings. With these devices, computer tasks can originate from users' ongoing real-world activities rather than solely from explicit instructions. Through first-person observations, agents can identify objects and activities relevant to user requests and ground digital tasks in the surrounding context. We call this interaction paradigm Ego Use . However, first-person observations are limited by the wearer's viewpoint and may provide incomplete or ambiguous evidence of ongoing activities. As new observations arrive, agents may need to revise their understanding of the physical context and user intent, and reassess whether prior digital actions remain valid. Whether current agents can reliably handle these changes remains insufficiently evaluated. We introduce EgoUseBench , a benchmark for evaluating Ego Use across three interaction settings with different levels of first-person context. Computer-Use relies on explicit instructions, Offline Ego Use provides prerecorded first-person context before execution, and Online Ego Use provides continuous observations as user intent evolves. Based on over 74 hours of real-world first-person recordings, we construct 693 tasks across the three interaction settings. To capture task evolution, we track first-person observations, user requirements, and website state separately. We further group tasks by how information changes during execution, resulting in three types: Graft (revised user requirements), Refresh (new first-person observations), and Clarify (agent-initiated information seeking). We evaluate several advanced models and find that average success rates in Online Ego Use are 26.3% lower than in Computer-Use. This result reveals the difficulty of keeping task execution aligned with evolving first-person context and user intent.

title: AIRIS: Benchmarking Social Embodied Intelligence in Egocentric Streaming Videos

details.title: AIRIS: Benchmarking Social Embodied Intelligence in Egocentric Streaming Videos
details.abstract: Embodied agents operating around people must not only recognize social cues, but also decide when the available evidence is sufficient, whether to intervene, and how to respond without violating social norms. Existing benchmarks typically evaluate these abilities in isolation or with access to completed videos, obscuring where an online social decision fails. We introduce AIRIS, a causal streaming benchmark that formulates social embodied intelligence as a time-anchored chain of Attention, Intention, Reaction, and Interaction (A-I-R-I). AIRIS contains 8,000 expert-curated questions grounded in 357 egocentric clips across 11 context categories and 36 capability dimensions. At each query, models receive only the observation prefix available at that time; decision-aware metrics reward calibrated waiting and complete reactions while penalizing premature commitment. Evaluating 45 proprietary and open-source general-purpose, embodied, streaming-video, and omni-modal models reveals fragmented and temporally miscalibrated competence. General-purpose VLMs excel at passive cue grounding and intent recognition, whereas embodied specialists lead on isolated reaction sub-decisions; yet across all families, models frequently guess intents before sufficient evidence emerges and fail to jointly align intervention timing, action domain, and concrete execution within the same episode. AIRIS thus provides a diagnostic foundation for bridging the gap between passive social perception and reliable embodied interaction.
